finding.title: Failed retry is swallowed, so the order is marked paid and shipped

other.title: Retrying every error can charge the card twice

findings.title: Failed retry is swallowed, so the order is marked paid and shipped
findings.scenario: The gateway rejects both charge attempts (for example, card declined). The inner catch only logs, then the code runs `return { ...order, status: 'paid' }`. In src/orders.js:5-6, `charged.status === 'paid'` is true, so `warehouse.ship` runs for an order nobody paid for. Before this change the error propagated and nothing shipped.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No tests exist: Grep for charge/idempot finds only src/payments.js and src/orders.js. Nothing after the catch checks whether either attempt worked. The intent was to give up after one retry, which means rethrowing.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "charge|idempot" across the repo: the only caller is src/orders.js:4-6, which ships when status === 'paid'

findings.title: Retrying every error can charge the card twice
findings.scenario: The first charge goes through at the gateway, but the response times out or a network error is thrown. The catch then calls charge again with no idempotency key, and the customer pays order.total twice.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The catch retries on any error without checking whether it can be retried. No idempotency key is passed (Grep for 'idempot' finds nothing). No test covers the retry path.

findings.title: No tests for the new retry behavior
findings.scenario: Three paths have no tests: success on the first attempt, success on the retry, and failure on both attempts. That is why the swallowed-failure bug above was not caught.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test files exist in the repo.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "charge" repo-wide: matches only in src/payments.js and src/orders.js

finding.title: Search term is interpolated into SQL, allowing SQL injection

other.title: LIKE wildcards in the search term are not escaped

findings.title: Search term is interpolated into SQL, allowing SQL injection
findings.quote: `SELECT id, name, email FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE '%${term}%' ORDER BY id LIMIT $1`,
findings.scenario: Request with q=x' OR 1=1; DROP TABLE customers; -- or q=' UNION SELECT id, password, email FROM users -- is passed unchanged from query.q into the SQL string, so it can read or destroy arbitrary data. A name that contains an apostrophe, like O'Brien, also causes a syntax error.
findings.whyNotPrevented: customersHandler passes query.q straight through without checking it, and the term is not bound as a parameter even though the same query already uses $1 for limit. No tests cover searchCustomers.

findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing escapes % or _ before the ILIKE pattern is built.

finding.title: cheapestFirst sorts the shared cached catalog in place, so later 'newest' lists show the most expensive items

findings.title: cheapestFirst sorts the shared cached catalog in place, so later 'newest' lists show the most expensive items
findings.scenario: loadCatalog caches one catalog object at module level (src/catalog.js:5) and returns it on every call. The first homePage call works, because newest is computed before the sort. That call then reorders cache.items by price. On the second request, listProducts(catalog).slice(-4) returns the 4 most expensive products as 'newest', not the 4 most recently added. Any other code that relies on the original order of catalog.items breaks in the same way.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Array.prototype.sort changes the array it is called on. listProducts returns a filtered copy, but featuredDeals passes catalog.items directly. There are no tests in the repo (Glob **/*.test.*: no files), and nothing makes the items read-only.

finding.title: Sort comparator returns a boolean, so topPlayers does not sort by points

findings.title: Sort comparator returns a boolean, so topPlayers does not sort by points
findings.scenario: board [{player:'a',points:1},{player:'b',points:5},{player:'c',points:3},{player:'d',points:9}] with count 3. The comparator only returns true (1) or false (0) and never a negative number, so Array.prototype.sort cannot move b ahead of a. V8's TimSort returns the original order, giving a, b, c instead of d, b, c. The leaderboard shows the wrong players.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Array.prototype.sort accepts any comparator without a type check. The repo has no tests that call topPlayers.

finding.title: getDay() checks for Monday, not the first day of the month

other.title: No test for the first-of-month billing condition

findings.title: getDay() checks for Monday, not the first day of the month
findings.scenario: In JavaScript, Date.prototype.getDay() returns the day of the week (0 is Sunday, 1 is Monday). On Monday 2026-10-05 every account is billed. On Thursday 2026-10-01 nobody is billed. So accounts get billed about four times a month and never on the 1st unless it happens to be a Monday. The check should be getDate() === 1, or getUTCDate() === 1 if billing should follow UTC.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test calls runDailyJobs. Grep finds it only where it is defined, and nothing in the code checks which date is used.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "getDate|getUTCDate|runDailyJobs|createInvoice": runDailyJobs appears only at src/scheduler.js:3, with no tests and no getDate usage

findings.title: Off-by-one `end` drops the last item of the list
findings.scenario: With 45 items, page 3 gives start=40 and end=min(60,44)=44. slice(40,44) returns 4 items, so item 45 is never shown, and the label reads 'Showing 41 to 44 of 45'. With exactly 20 items, page 1 returns 19 items and says 'Showing 1 to 19 of 20'.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No tests cover paginate. slice already treats `end` as exclusive, so subtracting 1 from length loses a row.

findings.title: Range label is wrong for an empty list or a page past the end

findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing clamps start or handles an empty list, and no tests exist.

findings.title: page=0 or a negative page now gives a negative start
findings.scenario: A client still using the old 0-based pages sends ?page=0. That gives start=-20 and end=0, so slice(-20,0) returns [] and the label reads 'Showing -19 to 0 of 45'. NaN from ?page=abc also produces a 'Showing NaN to NaN' label.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Query input is never validated, and the switch from 0-based to 1-based pages has no check that page is at least 1.

findings.title: No tests for paginate or the new range label

findings.title: Cache key leaves out currency, so the first currency's price is returned for every currency
findings.scenario: priceIn(client, {id: 1, priceCents: 1000}, 'EUR') caches 920. A later priceIn(client, same product, 'JPY') returns 920 instead of about 150000, because the lookup only checks product.id.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing checks or tests the key. The Map is keyed only by product.id, but the result depends on currency too.

findings.title: Cached prices never expire, so they ignore later rate changes and product price edits
findings.scenario: The EUR rate moves from 0.92 to 0.95, or product.priceCents goes from 1000 to 1200. priceIn keeps returning the old 920 until the process restarts.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The module-level Map has no TTL and no invalidation. The key also does not include priceCents, so a changed price on the same product.id is never seen.

findings.title: Cache has no size limit and is keyed per product rather than per rate
findings.scenario: With many products the Map grows without limit for the life of the process. Each new product still calls the rates service even when that currency's rate was already fetched. Caching the result of fetchRate per currency would cut more calls and use less memory.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing evicts entries.

findings.title: No tests for the cache hit and miss paths
findings.scenario: Tests would have caught the missing currency in the key. The module-level Map also carries state from one test to the next.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The diff adds no tests.

findings.title: Cache key ignores the client, so different clients share cached rates
findings.scenario: Suppose two callers pass different clients, for example different rate-service endpoints or tenants, and ask for the same currency within 10 minutes. The second caller gets the first caller's rate and its own client is never called.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The cache is a module-level Map keyed only by currency. Nothing ties an entry to the client that fetched it. The repo has no tests.

findings.title: Concurrent misses for the same currency each call the rates service
findings.scenario: When the cache is cold or just expired, N concurrent priceIn calls for EUR all miss and send N requests to the rates service. That works against the goal of cutting calls.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Only the resolved value is cached, after the await. In-flight promises are not cached, so callers that arrive during the fetch don't share it.

findings.title: An invalid or missing rate is cached for the full ten minutes
findings.scenario: If the rates service returns a body without `rate`, `undefined` is cached. Every priceIn call for that currency then returns NaN for 10 minutes, even after the service recovers.
findings.whyNotPrevented: fetchRate returns response.rate without checking it, and cachedRate stores whatever it gets.

findings.scenario: There is no check for a hit before 10 minutes, a refetch at or after 10 minutes, or keys kept separate per currency. A boundary or off-by-one mistake would ship unnoticed.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The repo has no test files and package.json has no test script.

finding.title: TTL in seconds is added to a millisecond timestamp, so sessions expire about 1000x too early

other.title: A non-numeric TTL setting makes sessions never expire

findings.title: TTL in seconds is added to a millisecond timestamp, so sessions expire about 1000x too early
findings.scenario: With the default SESSION_TTL_SECONDS=1800, a session created at Date.now() gets expiresAt = now + 1800 ms. It expires after 1.8 seconds instead of 30 minutes, so getSession returns null almost at once and logins effectively stop working.
findings.whyNotPrevented: config.sessionTtlSeconds is a plain Number with no unit type. The repo has no tests: only package.json, src/config.js and src/sessions.js exist.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "sessionTtl": src/config.js:2 sessionTtlSeconds: Number(process.env.SESSION_TTL_SECONDS ?? 1800); src/sessions.js:8 adds it to now = Date.now() (milliseconds)

findings.title: A non-numeric TTL setting makes sessions never expire
findings.scenario: If SESSION_TTL_SECONDS is set to something that is not a number (for example '30m'), Number() returns NaN, so expiresAt is NaN. NaN <= now is false, so the session never expires. Nothing checks the config value when it is read.
findings.whyNotPrevented: config.js does not validate the Number() result, and the expiry check treats NaN as 'not expired'.

findings.title: Expiry logic has no tests even though it takes an injectable `now`
findings.scenario: A test that creates a session at now=0 and reads it at now=1799s and now=1800s would have caught the units bug. The repo has no test files.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test directory or test files exist.
findings.measuredBy: Glob "**/*.{js,json}": only package.json, src/config.js, src/sessions.js
